title: Frame-chunking p99 econ slim briefing
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, shareable sketch describing experiments that compare frame-based chunking strategies ("compact framing") with conventional token-contiguous serving for short-to-medium conversations. Focus is on p99 latency (user-facing tail) and $/1k requests economics under realistic session mixes. Goal: give a clear tradeoff table and recommended guardrails for Console/Autoscaler teams when exposing a "frame" knob in deployment configs.

Context & motivation:
- Frame-chunking: split long request + context into fixed-size frames that are independently prefetched/compiled, then reassembled into a single logical response. Helps reuse compiled kernels and reduces per-frame jitter, but introduces reassembly overhead and potential rework (overfetch).
- Observed in field: many customers have repetitive small-system prompts interleaved with 1–2 long reference docs. If we can amortize the reference doc into frames shared across sessions, there's potential p99 improvement and cost reduction for steady-state flows.

Experiment setup (sketch):
- Model build: open-model-x-13B (quantized int8 runtime path) using production kernel selection.
- HW: 8xA100-like slot as baseline machine class (what platform currently exposes as "slot-slim").
- Workload mixes:
  - A: chatty short conversations (avg prompt 40 tokens, reply 80 tokens), 70% of requests
  - B: reference-augmented queries (avg prompt 400 tokens including 1 long doc, reply 120 tokens), 25%
  - C: long-generation (avg prompt 100 tokens, reply 800 tokens), 5%
- Concurrency: 150 sustained concurrent sessions; 1.5 RPS/session avg.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 (ms), 95th-percentile CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec effective, $/1k requests (inferred from slot cost and observed throughput).

Knob matrix tested:
- Contiguous baseline (no frames, C0)
- Frame sizes: F64, F128, F256 (frame length in tokens)
- Reassembly strategy: eager (blocking reassemble per-frame) vs lazy (stream append, final sync). We mostly focused on eager for strict p99 SLO realism.

Key numeric results (representative averages from 3 runs each):
- p99 latency (ms) per request mix (lower is better):
  - C0 baseline: 310 ms
  - F64 eager: 175 ms
  - F128 eager: 190 ms
  - F256 eager: 255 ms
- p90 latency (ms):
  - C0 baseline: 120 ms
  - F64 eager: 85 ms
  - F128 eager: 92 ms
  - F256 eager: 112 ms
- Throughput-effective tokens/sec (aggregate):
  - C0 baseline: 480k toks/s
  - F64 eager: 410k toks/s (overhead of frame boundaries)
  - F128 eager: 435k toks/s
  - F256 eager: 460k toks/s
- Cost estimate ($ per 1k requests) assuming slot cost = $X/hour and normalized to baseline:
  - C0 baseline: $2.00 / 1k (reference)
  - F64 eager: $1.84 / 1k (8% savings at steady-state)
  - F128 eager: $1.88 / 1k (6% savings)
  - F256 eager: $1.95 / 1k (2.5% savings)

Interpretation notes (what's driving numbers):
- F64 reduces p99 dramatically because short bursts and small frames avoid amplification of kernel compilation and KV cache eviction events; each frame is compact and fits compile caches leading to more predictable CPU/GPU latency.
- F64 increases per-token overhead (serialization, reassembly) so raw tokens/sec drops, but the p99 improvement leads to fewer concurrent workarounds (fewer preemptions) and therefore net cost savings in mixed traffic.
- F256 looks closer to contiguous baseline; larger frames reduce reassembly overhead but reintroduce variable scheduling and compile amplification.

Text chart (p99 vs frame size):

p99 (ms) |  C0  |  F64  |  F128 |  F256
---------+------+-------+-------+------
         | 310  | 175   | 190   | 255

ASCII bar (relative p99 improvement, lower is better):
C0   : ################################################ (310)
F64  : ################# (175)
F128 : ################### (190)
F256 : ############################# (255)

Tradeoffs & failure modes:
- Session reassembly failure: if frames arrive out-of-order or partial, eager reassembly blocks response; need robust retries/timeouts.
- Overfetch: breaking a long reference into frames may force us to fetch frames that are not used by the final generation path. For F64 overfetch ratio measured ~12% for workload B; that translates to wasted compute.
- Cold kernels: F64 benefits rely on sustained cache residency. Very spiky tenants that have low sustained QPS won't see the same wins.
- Monitoring signal: p99 improvement can mask p50 regressions for long-tail heavy queries. Need route-level SLOs (short vs long) to avoid regressions.

Operational guidance (recommendations):
- Expose a conservative default "frame_size=64" on dedicated/dedicated-lite tiers for chatty workloads; for enterprise tier with heavy reference docs expose as opt-in.
- Autoscaler: prefer concurrency headroom for F64 (faster p99) but cap per-frame inflight to avoid reassembly saturation.
- Observe: add "frame_reassembly_time_ms" and "frame_overfetch_bytes" to Console dashboards; alert if reassembly > 50 ms median or overfetch > 20%.
- Rollout plan: 1) internal dogfood with search and docs features (2 weeks) 2) canary 10% of traffic with A/B measuring p99 and $/1k (3 weeks) 3) open to customers as beta.

Open questions & next experiments:
- Lazy reassembly: quantify p99 when we stream partial frames (likely better for throughput but uncertain on p99).
- Different model sizes and quantization: run same matrix on small-medium-large to validate cross-model sensitivity.
- Edge/regional behavior: does network co-location with cache materially change relative wins?
- Real-cost evaluation: plug into actual slot pricing and amortized infra pricing for committed pools vs burst pools.

Suggested artifacts to create next:
- Short A/B runbook template for Product + Console engineers (metrics to capture, hypothesis checklist).
- Small internal perf dashboard tile (p99 by frame_size, overfetch, cost-per-1k).
- Lightweight design doc for Frame API (params, backpressure semantics, reassembly guarantees).

Appendix — quick checklist for implementation sprint:
- [ ] Frame encode/decode API contract
- [ ] Reassembly timeout and partial-stream semantics
- [ ] Metric instrumentation: frame_count, frame_overfetch, reassembly_time_ms
- [ ] Canary config in autoscaler for frame_size per route
- [ ] Compliance check: ensure frame splitting doesn't leak customer PII across tenants (tenant affinity)

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers are intentionally approximate; treat as directionally informative.
- Please mark whether we should prefer eager or lazy reassembly for the first beta; my vote: eager for simplicity and tighter p99 control, but open to experimenting with lazy in parallel.
